name: THE GOAT TELL IT ON THE MOUNTAIN BURGER (comes with goat cheese)

recipe.history:
Goat cheese — known as chèvre in French — carries one of the oldest pedigrees in the entire world of dairy. Goats were among the first animals domesticated by humans, with evidence of goat herding dating back over ten thousand years to the Zagros Mountains of what is now Iran and the fertile crescent of the Middle East. Long before cows were widely milked, goats provided sustenance to nomadic and semi-nomadic peoples across the Mediterranean, the Middle East, and North Africa. The ancient Greeks prized goat's milk and its pressed curds; Roman texts document the trading of fresh goat cheeses along the roads of the empire. In France, the Loire Valley became particularly celebrated for chèvre — the climate, the soil, and the goats themselves producing milk with a distinctive tang and minerality that aged well into firm rounds or was eaten fresh and spreadable. By the medieval period, French monasteries were producing refined chèvre in styles that still bear their regional names today: Crottin de Chavignol, Valençay, Sainte-Maure de Touraine. The flavor profile of goat cheese — bright, lactic, earthy, and faintly grassy — is a direct reflection of the goat's browsing diet and the smaller fat globules in its milk, which create a softer, creamier curd than cow's milk.

Goat cheese arrived in American consciousness slowly, carried first by immigrant communities from France, the Mediterranean, and the Middle East who kept small goat herds and made fresh cheese as they always had. For much of the twentieth century it remained a specialty item, found in ethnic grocery stores and farmers' markets but largely absent from mainstream American kitchens. That changed in the 1970s and 1980s when the American artisan cheese movement began to gather momentum. California cheesemakers like Laura Chenel — who sent samples to Alice Waters at Chez Panisse in 1979 — helped introduce the American dining public to fresh chèvre as an ingredient worthy of fine cooking. Waters put a warm goat cheese salad on the Chez Panisse menu and changed the way Americans thought about the cheese forever. From there, chèvre migrated into pastas, pizzas, and eventually burgers, where chefs discovered that its creamy tang cut beautifully through the richness of a beef patty, acting almost like a bright acidic counterpoint without the sharpness of a vinegar-based condiment. The burger world, always hungry for textural and flavor contrast, welcomed goat cheese with open arms.

I remember the first time I put goat cheese on a burger with any real intention behind it. It was a late Sunday in October, the kind of afternoon where the light comes in sideways and turns everything golden and a little sad. I had half a log of chèvre in the refrigerator, left over from a dinner party the night before, and a pound of eighty-twenty ground chuck that needed to be used. I crumbled the goat cheese directly onto the patty the last two minutes of cooking, watched it soften and slump and begin to meld with the crust of the beef. I had sliced beets roasted the day before, a handful of arugula, and a smear of honey on the top bun. The combination hit me hard — the funkiness of the cheese, the sweetness of the honey and beet, the peppery bite of the arugula, all of it riding on the savory depth of the medium-rare patty beneath. I stood at the counter eating it because I didn't want to waste a single second of its temperature getting to the table. That burger taught me that goat cheese doesn't just belong on salads; it belongs anywhere that needs brightness and body in the same breath.

To cook a burger to medium rare is not a preference — it is a commitment to the ingredient itself. Ground beef, especially a blend with sufficient fat, is transformed at 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit into something that is simultaneously tender and structured, juicy and coherent. The interior stays pink and yielding; the fat has begun to render but has not fully escaped the meat; the proteins have set just enough to hold everything together without squeezing dry. Going beyond this temperature — into the 150s and 160s that constitute medium-well and well-done — is to drive out the moisture that makes a burger worth eating, to tighten the muscle fibers into something closer to a meat puck than a patty. People who ask for well-done burgers are, consciously or not, asking for the flavor cooked out of their food. A medium-rare burger finished with goat cheese is a thing of specific perfection: the cool creaminess of the cheese meets the warm, blushing center, and together they create a temperature and flavor gradient that no overcooked patty can replicate.
ingredients: 2 medium beets, roasted, peeled, and sliced
1/2 red onion, thinly sliced into rings
1 tbsp red wine vinegar (for quick-pickling onions)
neutral oil (canola or vegetable) for cooking
instructions: 1. Roast the beets: Preheat oven to 400°F (205°C). Toss beet halves with olive oil, salt, and pepper. Wrap in foil and roast 45–50 minutes until fork-tender. Cool, peel, and slice into 1/4-inch rounds. Set aside.

2. Quick-pickle the red onion: Combine red wine vinegar, sugar, and a pinch of salt in a small bowl. Add the sliced red onion rings and toss to coat. Let sit at room temperature at least 30 minutes, stirring occasionally.

3. Make the buns: In a large bowl, whisk together warm milk, sugar, and yeast. Let stand 5 minutes until foamy. Add softened butter and egg; whisk to combine. Add bread flour and salt. Mix until a shaggy dough forms, then knead on a lightly floured surface for 8–10 minutes until smooth and elastic. Place in an oiled bowl, cover, and let rise in a warm spot for 1 hour or until doubled.

4. Divide dough into 4 equal portions. Shape each into a smooth ball, flatten slightly, and place on a parchment-lined baking sheet 3 inches apart. Cover loosely with plastic wrap and let rise 30–40 minutes until puffed.
5. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush buns with egg wash (egg yolk + milk). Sprinkle with sesame seeds if using. Bake 15–18 minutes until deep golden brown. Cool on a wire rack before slicing.

6. Prepare the goat cheese topping: In a small bowl, combine crumbled chèvre with fresh thyme leaves, lemon zest, and olive oil. Gently fold together — you want it mixed but still textured, not completely smooth. Set aside at room temperature.
7. Make the honey-herb aioli: Whisk together mayonnaise, wildflower honey, lemon juice, Dijon mustard, and a pinch of flaky salt. Taste and adjust seasoning. Refrigerate until ready to serve.

8. Form the patties: Divide the ground beef into 4 equal portions (about 175g each). Gently form into patties approximately 4 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick. Press a shallow dimple in the center of each patty with your thumb. Season generously on both sides with kosher salt and black pepper just before cooking.

9. Heat a cast-iron skillet or heavy grill pan over high heat until very hot, approximately 3 minutes. Add a thin film of neutral oil. Place patties in the pan and do not move them for 3 minutes — you are building a crust.

10. Flip the patties once. Cook for 2 more minutes. In the last 90 seconds of cooking, spoon the herbed goat cheese mixture generously over each patty. Tent loosely with foil to encourage the cheese to warm and soften without running completely off. Target internal temperature: 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Remove from heat and rest 3 minutes.
11. While patties rest, lightly toast the buns cut-side down in the residual fat in the pan for 60–90 seconds until golden.

12. Assemble the burgers: Spread honey-herb aioli on both the bottom and top buns. Place a patty with its softened goat cheese on the bottom bun. Layer 2–3 roasted beet slices over the cheese. Add a small handful of baby arugula. Top with a few pickled red onion rings. Close with the top bun and press gently. Serve immediately.
